subject: english
passage:
Every year, a week before Makar Sankranti, the narrow lane behind the vegetable market in Nagpur fills with colour. This is where Shabbir Bhai has made kites for forty-one years. His shop is no wider than a doorway, but from it come kites of every size, from tiny ones the length of a hand to great ones that need two people to launch.

Shabbir Bhai will not use plastic. Plastic kites fly well enough, he says, but they never rot away, and every February he sees them hanging in the trees along the road, faded and torn, months after the festival has ended. His own kites are made of thin paper and split bamboo, and if one is lost it returns quietly to the soil.

Younger shopkeepers in the same lane sell plastic kites by the hundred and make more money than he does. Shabbir Bhai knows this. He shrugs when it is mentioned, and goes back to trimming a length of bamboo with a blade worn thin by use. His customers, he says, come back each year, and their children come after them. That is a kind of profit too.
question: For how long has Shabbir Bhai been making kites?
options: Forty-one years
Four years
Fourteen years
Since last Makar Sankranti
hint: The second sentence of the passage gives the number of years directly.

subject: english
passageTitle: The Night the Lights Went Out
passage:
The power failed at half past eight, in the middle of Anaya's homework. For a moment the whole colony was silent. Then, one by one, the sounds arrived: a door opening, somebody laughing on a balcony, a child asking a question in a high voice.

Anaya climbed to the terrace with her grandmother. She had lived in this flat all her life and had never once looked up and seen more than a handful of stars. Now the sky above the colony was crowded with them, thick as spilt salt, right down to the rooftops.

'They were always there,' her grandmother said. 'You could not see them because of us.' Below, the generators began to cough and catch. One tube light flickered on, then a second. By the time Anaya looked up again, the faintest stars had already gone.
question: At what time did the power fail?
options: Early in the morning
At midnight
Half past nine
Half past eight
hint: The very first sentence of the passage gives the time.

subject: english
passage:
A stepwell is not a well as most people picture one. Instead of a round mouth and a bucket on a rope, it is a long flight of steps cut down into the earth, storey after storey, until the water is reached. In the dry regions of Gujarat and Rajasthan, hundreds of them were built between the sixth and the nineteenth centuries.

The stepwell at Adalaj, near Ahmedabad, goes five storeys down. Carved pillars line each level, and the air grows cooler with every flight of steps. Even at noon in May, when the land above is too hot to stand on, the lowest level stays pleasant. Villagers once gathered there in the middle of the day, and the well became a meeting place as much as a water source.

When piped water arrived in the last century, most stepwells fell out of use. Many filled with rubbish or dried up as the water table sank. A few, like Adalaj, are now protected. Visitors climb down them for the carvings, and are surprised, halfway, by the cold.
question: How many storeys does the stepwell at Adalaj go down?
options: Nineteen
Five
Three
Nine
hint: The second paragraph opens with the number.

subject: english
passage:
In a laboratory in New Zealand, a crow was shown a tall glass tube with a little water at the bottom. Floating on the water was a scrap of meat, too far down for the bird to reach with its beak. Beside the tube lay a small heap of pebbles.

The crow looked at the tube. Then it picked up a pebble, dropped it in, and watched. The water rose by a fraction. It dropped in a second pebble, and a third. After eight pebbles the meat had risen far enough to be taken, and the crow took it.

What interested the scientists was not that the crow got the meat. It was that the bird had never been taught this and had not seen another crow do it. Later tests made the puzzle harder: when the pebbles were replaced with pieces of foam that did not raise the water, most crows tried them once or twice, then stopped and looked for something heavier.
question: How many pebbles did the crow drop in before it could reach the meat?
options: Eighteen
Three
Eight
Two
hint: The second paragraph gives the number directly.

subject: english
passageTitle: The Letter That Took Nine Years
passage:
In 2013, a postman in Kolkata delivered a letter that had been posted in 2004. It had slipped behind a shelf in a sorting office and lay there, unnoticed, for nine years. When the shelf was finally moved during repairs, the letter came out with the dust.

It was addressed to a woman named Sujata, and it was from her brother, who had written to say he was coming home for Durga Puja. By the time it arrived he had visited many times, and the family had a new address; the postman traced them through a neighbour who had lived on the street for thirty years.

Sujata said afterwards that she had known all along that her brother was coming that year — he had telephoned. But she kept the letter anyway. It was the only thing she owned, she said, in which he described the journey he was planning, in his own hand, before he made it.
question: Where had the letter been lying for nine years?
options: Behind a shelf in a sorting office
At Sujata's old address
In a postbox on the street
In her brother's house
hint: The first paragraph says exactly where it had slipped.

subject: english
passage:
In 2002, a chemistry professor in Madurai named Rajagopalan Vasudevan tried something odd. He shredded waste plastic — the sort that blows about in streets and blocks drains — heated it, and mixed it into the hot bitumen used for surfacing roads.

The result surprised him. The plastic coated the stone chips and helped them bind, and the road that came out was harder to crack than an ordinary one. It stood up better to heavy rain, and it used up plastic that had no other use and would otherwise have been burnt or buried.

The method is now used in many Indian states, and thousands of kilometres of road have been laid this way. It is not a complete answer to the plastic problem: a road cannot swallow every bag and bottle a country throws away, and the plastic is not gone, only locked in place. But it turns a nuisance into something a village can drive on.
question: What did Professor Vasudevan mix into hot bitumen?
options: Shredded waste plastic
River sand
Sawdust from timber mills
Crushed glass
hint: The first paragraph names the material exactly.

The result surprised him. The plastic coated the stone chips and helped them bind, and the road that came out was harder to crack than an ordinary one. It stood up better to heavy rain, and it used up plastic that had no other use and would otherwise have been burnt or buried.

The method is now used in many Indian states, and thousands of kilometres of road have been laid this way. It is not a complete answer to the plastic problem: a road cannot swallow every bag and bottle a country throws away, and the plastic is not gone, only locked in place. But it turns a nuisance into something a village can drive on.
question: According to the passage, how did the plastic improve the road?
options: It allowed the road to be laid without any bitumen
It coated the stone chips, helped them bind, and made the road harder to crack
It made the road softer and more comfortable to walk on
It made the road cheaper to light at night
hint: The second paragraph lists what the plastic did to the mixture.

subject: english
passage:
Radhika Menon's library has no building. It has a bicycle, two wooden crates bolted over the back wheel, and about ninety books. Three afternoons a week she rides it out to the hamlets beyond her village in Kerala, where the nearest proper library is eleven kilometres away.

The rules are simple. A child may borrow one book and must return it before taking another. Nothing is written down. In four years, Radhika says, she has lost six books, and four of those came back eventually — one after eight months, carried to her gate by a boy who had moved to another village and remembered.

She is often asked why she does not ask for identity cards or a deposit. Her answer is that a deposit would keep out exactly the children she rides out to reach, and that six books in four years is a cheap price for a system that no child is afraid of.
question: How far away is the nearest proper library from the hamlets Radhika visits?
options: Four kilometres
Eleven kilometres
Eight kilometres
Ninety kilometres
hint: The distance is given at the end of the first paragraph.

passage:
When the first heavy rain of the monsoon falls on the dry plains of eastern India, something strange happens in the flooded fields. Fish appear in water that held none the day before — in ditches, in paddy fields, sometimes in puddles beside the road.

Some have been carried there by the flood. But the climbing perch does something else. It can breathe air through a special organ above its gills, and it can push itself overland on its stiff fins and gill covers, travelling from a drying pool to a fuller one. It moves slowly and awkwardly, and it can survive out of water for several hours.

Farmers in Bihar and Odisha have known this for generations and are not surprised by it. What surprises visitors is the direction: the fish are not being washed downhill by the water. They are going the other way, uphill, towards it.
question: What allows the climbing perch to breathe out of water?
options: Very large gills
A special organ above its gills
Its stiff fins
A layer of mud on its skin
hint: The second paragraph names the organ and where it sits.

subject: english
passageTitle: The Clock That Was Always Wrong
passage:
The clock on the tower at the centre of our town has been eleven minutes fast for as long as anyone can remember. Every few years somebody writes to the municipality about it, and every few years nothing happens.

The odd thing is that the town has arranged itself around the mistake. The bus to the district headquarters leaves at what the tower calls a quarter past nine, and everybody who catches it knows to arrive at the tower's quarter past. Shops shut by the tower. School bells are set by it. A visitor once corrected his watch by the tower and missed his train by eleven minutes.

Last year a young engineer offered to fix it without charge. The shopkeepers thanked him and asked him not to. If the clock were made right, they said, then for a week or two everybody in town would be wrong.
question: By how much is the tower clock fast?
options: An hour
A quarter of an hour
Nine minutes
Eleven minutes
hint: The first sentence gives the figure.

passage:
In a village in Karnataka, in a room off her kitchen, Lakshmamma keeps seeds. There are more than seven hundred varieties in her collection, stored in earthen pots and old tins, each labelled in her own writing: sixty kinds of rice, twenty of millet, beans, gourds, greens whose names do not appear in any catalogue.

Most of these plants are grown by nobody now. Farmers buy a few high-yielding varieties instead, which give more grain but need more water and more chemicals. Lakshmamma does not argue against those varieties. She argues against having only those varieties.

Her reason is simple and hard to answer. A field of one kind of rice can be wiped out by one disease. A field of many kinds cannot. She gives her seeds away free to anyone who will plant them and bring back twice as many, and in thirty years she has never run short.
question: How many varieties of seed does Lakshmamma keep?
options: Exactly sixty
More than seven hundred
About twenty
Thirty
hint: The first paragraph gives the total before listing some of the kinds.

passageTitle: The Boy Who Waited for the Train
passage:
The railway line ran past the bottom of our field, and the Delhi mail passed at twenty to six every evening. My cousin Vinod, who was seven that summer, went down to the fence to watch it every single day, and every day he waved.

For weeks nobody waved back. The train went by at speed, a long blur of lit windows, and Vinod would stand a moment longer and then walk back up to the house without saying anything about it.

Then one evening in August the guard in the last carriage saw him, leaned out, and waved with his whole arm. Vinod said nothing at dinner. But he was at the fence again the next day twenty minutes early, and he had put on his good shirt.
question: At what time did the Delhi mail pass the field?
options: Eight in the evening
Twenty to six
Twenty past six
Five o'clock
hint: The first sentence gives the time the train passed.

passageTitle: The Honey Hunters of the Nilgiris
passage:
The Kurumba people of the Nilgiri hills have gathered wild honey from cliff faces for centuries. The nests of the rock bee hang from overhangs a hundred feet above the ground, and reaching them means climbing down a ladder of bamboo and forest rope, made on the spot and left to rot afterwards.

A hunter goes down with a smouldering bundle of leaves. The smoke does not harm the bees; it quiets them enough for the comb to be cut. Only part of each nest is taken. The rest is left so the colony can rebuild, and the same cliff can be harvested again the following year.

Younger Kurumba are learning the work more slowly than their parents did, and some of the old songs sung during the descent are now remembered by only a handful of people. The honey itself sells well in the cities below. It is the climb, and the knowledge of when not to take, that is harder to pass on.
question: How high above the ground do the rock bee nests hang?
options: About a hundred feet
At ground level
About ten feet

passageTitle: The Honey Hunters of the Nilgiris
passage:
The Kurumba people of the Nilgiri hills have gathered wild honey from cliff faces for centuries. The nests of the rock bee hang from overhangs a hundred feet above the ground, and reaching them means climbing down a ladder of bamboo and forest rope, made on the spot and left to rot afterwards.

A hunter goes down with a smouldering bundle of leaves. The smoke does not harm the bees; it quiets them enough for the comb to be cut. Only part of each nest is taken. The rest is left so the colony can rebuild, and the same cliff can be harvested again the following year.

Younger Kurumba are learning the work more slowly than their parents did, and some of the old songs sung during the descent are now remembered by only a handful of people. The honey itself sells well in the cities below. It is the climb, and the knowledge of when not to take, that is harder to pass on.

options: To keep the hunter warm on the cliff
To make smoke that quiets the bees
To light the hunter's way in the dark
To burn away the old nest
hint: The passage says what the smoke does, and what it does not do.
